title: The New Issues Puzzle
research_question: Do firms that issue equity—either through initial public offerings or seasoned equity offerings—deliver systematically lower long-run stock returns to investors than otherwise comparable firms that do not issue equity? If so, can this underperformance be explained by differences in firm size, book-to-market ratios, beta risk, or long-term return reversals, or does it reflect a distinct 'new issues' phenomenon potentially tied to firms timing offerings when their shares are overvalued?
data_description: The study uses a sample of 4,753 U.S. initial public offerings and 3,702 nonutility seasoned equity offerings (involving at least some primary shares) conducted between 1970 and 1990, by firms subsequently listed on Nasdaq, Amex, or NYSE. IPO data are drawn from Investment Dealer's Digest (1970–1974), Going Public: The IPO Reporter (1975–1984), and IDD Information Services and Securities Data Co. (1985–1990). SEO data come from SEC registered offering statistics, Loderer-Sheehan-Kadlec (1980–1984), and Securities Data Co. Stock returns are obtained from CRSP daily Nasdaq and Amex-NYSE tapes; book values come from COMPUSTAT, Moody's OTC Industrial Manual, prospectuses, and IDD/SDC. Key variables include three- and five-year buy-and-hold returns, monthly returns, market capitalization, book-to-market ratios, and an issuer indicator. The unit of observation is the issuing firm (matched to a size-comparable nonissuer) or, in time-series tests, the firm-month.
institutional_context: During 1970–1990, U.S. equity issuance volume fluctuated dramatically, with pronounced 'hot' and 'cold' markets for both IPOs and SEOs. Many firms going public were young growth firms with rapid prior earnings or sales growth, while seasoned issuers typically conducted offerings after substantial share-price runups (averaging 72 percent in the year before an SEO). Announcements of seasoned offerings were known to trigger an average price drop of about 3 percent. The introduction of Nasdaq in February 1971 expanded the venues available to newly public companies, and CRSP began reporting Nasdaq returns in December 1972. The setting allows comparing the post-offering performance of issuers against otherwise similar nonissuing firms over multi-year horizons, exploiting variation in issuance timing, the heterogeneity between IPOs and SEOs, and across periods of high versus low aggregate issuance activity, to assess whether managers exploit transitory windows of opportunity to sell overvalued equity.
